name: Presubiculum
summary: The presubiculum is the strip of cortex between the subiculum and the entorhinal cortex on the medial surface of the parahippocampal gyrus, together with the parasubiculum forming the transition from the three-layered hippocampus to the six-layered cortex. It contains head-direction cells that signal which way the animal faces, receives the anterior thalamus and the retrosplenial cortex, and projects to the medial entorhinal cortex, so it supplies the compass that the entorhinal grid and the hippocampal place cells need. It is a small target but part of the medial temporal region injured in Alzheimer disease, in limbic encephalitis and in mesial temporal epilepsy, and it contributes to the spatial disorientation of those conditions.

anatomy.location: Narrow cortical zone on the upper medial surface of the parahippocampal gyrus, medial to the subiculum and lateral to the entorhinal cortex, running along the hippocampal formation from head to tail beside the hippocampal sulcus.

function: Presubicular neurons receive the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, whose head-direction signal derives from vestibular input via the mammillary bodies, together with the retrosplenial cortex and the subiculum, and they project this heading information to the medial entorhinal cortex and back to the anterior thalamus; the result is a stable compass that anchors the grid cells and place cells of the hippocampal map to the visual landmarks of the environment. The presubiculum also carries hippocampal output back to the retrosplenial cortex and receives a strong visual input from the parahippocampal cortex. Its damage produces loss of directional sense with preserved recognition of places.

bestView.label: presubiculum between the subiculum and the entorhinal cortex
medial parahippocampal transition cortex along the hippocampus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not separable from the subiculum and entorhinal cortex on clinical MRI; it occupies the medial lip of the parahippocampal gyrus beside the hippocampal sulcus on coronal images, identified by subfield atlases.

pathology.finding: Medial temporal atrophy involving the parahippocampal transition cortex with the entorhinal cortex; tau spreads through this zone from entorhinal to hippocampal fields.
Bilateral medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling including the parahippocampal cortex, with amnesia and disorientation.
Mammillary body and medial thalamic signal change disrupts the anterior thalamic input to the presubiculum, with loss of directional sense as part of the amnesia.

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of directional sense and heading
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the presubicular head-direction network
Disconnection of the retrosplenial-presubicular-entorhinal navigation circuit
Part of the entorhinal-hippocampal memory system

examination: Ask the patient to point toward home or toward a landmark from the clinic
Route learning and description of familiar routes
pearls: The head-direction cells of the presubiculum are the brain's compass; the vestibular system feeds them through the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus
Directional sense and place recognition are separable: retrosplenial-presubicular lesions lose the former
This transition cortex is the road along which Alzheimer tau travels from the entorhinal cortex into the hippocampus

pitfalls: Presubicular structures appear only in subfield atlases; a report that names them is describing atlas labels, not visible anatomy
